entries.2b0e31d5d80a88f7f32248859019d1ddc13b9b53: <div sID="gen5988" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="2Sam.3" sID="2Sam.3"/> <div eID="gen5988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5990" type="x-p"/> The battle between Joab and Abner did not end the controversy between the two houses of Saul and David, but it is in this chapter working towards a period. Here is, I. The gradual advance of David's interest, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The building up of his family, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.2-2Sam.3.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. III. Abner's quarrel with Ish-bosheth, and his treaty with David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6-2Sam.3.12">ver. 6-12</reference>. IV. The preliminaries settled, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.13-2Sam.3.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. V. Abner's undertaking and attempt to bring Israel over to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.17-2Sam.3.21">ver. 17-21</reference>. VI. The treacherous murder of Abner by Joab, when he was carrying on this matter, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.22-2Sam.3.27">ver. 22-27</reference>. VII. David's great concern and trouble for the death of Abner, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.28-2Sam.3.39">ver. 28-39</reference>.
entries.fa12a326a2093fbba0f82370367de74e38a678b3: <div eID="gen5990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5989" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Wives and Children. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen5991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker. <hi type="super">2</hi> And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; <hi type="super">3</hi> And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; <hi type="super">4</hi> And the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith; and the fifth, Shephatiah the son of Abital; <hi type="super">5</hi> And the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass, while there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, that Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul. <div eID="gen5991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5992" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The struggle that David had with the house of Saul before his settlement in the throne was completed, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Both sides contested. Saul's house, though beheaded and diminished, would not fall tamely. It is not strange between them, but one would wonder it should be a long war, when David's house had right on its side, and therefore God on its side; but, though truth and equity will triumph at last, God made for wise and holy ends prolonged the conflict. The length of this war tried the faith and patience of David, and made his establishment at last the more welcome to him. 2. David's side got ground. The house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker, lost places, lost men, sunk in its reputation, grew less considerable, and was foiled in every engagement. But the house of David grew stronger and stronger. Many deserted the declining cause of Saul's house, and prudently came into David's interest, being convinced that he would certainly win the day. The contest between grace and corruption in the hearts of believers, who are sanctified but in part, may fitly be compared to this recorded here. There is a long war between them, the flesh lusted against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh; but, as the work of sanctification is carried on, corruption, like the house of Saul, grows weaker and weaker; while grace, like the house of David, grows stronger and stronger, till it come to a perfect man, and judgment be brought forth unto victory. <div eID="gen5992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5993" type="x-p"/> II. The increase of his own house. Here is an account of six sons he had by six several wives, in the seven years he reigned in Hebron. Perhaps this is here mentioned as that which strengthened David's interest. Every child, whose welfare was embarked in the common safety, was a fresh security given to the commonwealth for his care of it. He that has his quiver filled with these arrows shall <hi type="italic">speak with his enemy in the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 5</reference>. As the death of Saul's sons weakened his interest, so the birth of David's strengthened his. 1. It was David's fault thus to multiply wives, contrary to the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.17">Deut. xvii. 17</reference>), and it was a bad example to his successors. 2. It does not appear that in these seven years he had above one son by each of these wives; some have had as numerous a progeny, and with much more honour and comfort, by one wife. 3. We read not that any of these sons came to be famous (three of them were infamous, Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah); we have therefore reason to rejoice with trembling in the building up of our families. 4. His son by Abigail is called <hi type="italic">Chileab</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.3">v. 3</reference>), whereas (<reference osisRef="1Chr.3.1">1 Chron. iii. 1</reference>) he is called <hi type="italic">Daniel.</hi> Bishop Patrick mentions the reason which the Hebrew doctors give for these names, that his first name was <hi type="italic">Daniel—God has judged me</hi> (namely, against Nabal), but David's enemies reproached him, and said, "It is Nabal's son, and not David's," to confute which calumny Providence so ordered it that, as he grew up, he became, in his countenance and features, extremely like David, and resembled him more than any of his children, upon which he gave him the name of <hi type="italic">Chileab,</hi> which signifies, <hi type="italic">like his father,</hi> or the father's picture. 5. Absalom's mother is said to be the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, a heathen prince. Perhaps David thereby hoped to strengthen his interest, but the issue of the marriage was one that proved his grief and shame. 6. The last is called <hi type="italic">David's wife,</hi> which therefore, some think, was Michal, his first and most rightful wife, called here by another name; and, though she had no child after she mocked David, she might have had before. <div eID="gen5993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5994" type="x-p"/> Thus was David's house strengthened; but it was Abner that <hi type="italic">made himself strong for the house of Saul,</hi> which is mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6">v. 6</reference>) to show that, if he failed them, they would fall of course.
entries.7bee1cc8cad2e654cfa85855cb4affd9ece1bc8b: <div eID="gen5994" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Abner Deserts to David. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen5995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And Saul had a concubine, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and <hi type="italic">Ishbosheth</hi> said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine? <hi type="super">8</hi> Then was Abner very wroth for the words of Ishbosheth, and said, <hi type="italic">Am</hi> I a dog's head, which against Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father, to his brethren, and to his friends, and have not delivered thee into the hand of David, that thou chargest me to day with a fault concerning this woman? <hi type="super">9</hi> So do God to Abner, and more also, except, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn to David, even so I do to him; <hi type="super">10</hi> To translate the kingdom from the house of Saul, and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beer-sheba. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, Whose <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land? saying <hi type="italic">also,</hi> Make thy league with me, and, behold, my hand <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> with thee, to bring about all Israel unto thee. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said, Well; I will make a league with thee: but one thing I require of thee, that is, Thou shalt not see my face, except thou first bring Michal Saul's daughter, when thou comest to see my face. <hi type="super">14</hi> And David sent messengers to Ishbosheth Saul's son, saying, Deliver <hi type="italic">me</hi> my wife Michal, which I espoused to me for an hundred foreskins of the Philistines. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Ishbosheth sent, and took her from <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband, <hi type="italic">even</hi> from Phaltiel the son of Laish. <hi type="super">16</hi> And her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim. Then said Abner unto him, Go, return. And he returned. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Abner had communication with the elders of Israel, saying, Ye sought for David in times past <hi type="italic">to be</hi> king over you: <hi type="super">18</hi> Now then do <hi type="italic">it:</hi> for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken of David, saying, By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines, and out of the hand of all their enemies. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Abner also spake in the ears of Benjamin: and Abner went also to speak in the ears of David in Hebron all that seemed good to Israel, and that seemed good to the whole house of Benjamin. <hi type="super">20</hi> So Abner came to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him. And David made Abner and the men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him a feast. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Abner said unto David, I will arise and go, and will gather all Israel unto my lord the king, that they may make a league with thee, and that thou mayest reign over all that thine heart desireth. And David sent Abner away; and he went in peace. <div eID="gen5995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5996" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Abner breaks with Ish-bosheth, and deserts his interest, upon a little provocation which Ish-bosheth unadvisedly gave him. God can serve his own purposes by the sins and follies of men. 1. Ish-bosheth accused Abner of no less a crime than debauching one of his father's concubines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">v. 7</reference>. Whether it was so or no does not appear, nor what ground he had for the suspicion: but, however it was, it would have been Ish-bosheth's prudence to be silent, considering how much it was his interest not to disoblige Abner. If the thing was false, and his jealousy groundless, it was very disingenuous and ungrateful to entertain unjust surmises of one who had ventured his all for him, and was certainly the best friend he had in the world. 2. Abner resented the charge very strongly. Whether he was guilty of the <hi type="italic">fault concerning this woman</hi> or no he does not say (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.8">v. 8</reference>), but we suspect he was guilty, for he does not expressly deny it; and, though he was, he lets Ish-bosheth know, (1.) That he scorned to be reproached with it by him, and would not take reproof at his hands. "What!" says Abner, "<hi type="italic">Am I a dog's head,</hi> a vile and contemptible animal, that thou exposest me thus? <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Is this my recompence for the kindness I have shown to thee and thy father's house, and the good services I have done you?" He magnifies the service with this, that it was against Judah, the tribe on which the crown was settled, and which would certainly have it at last, so that, in supporting the house of Saul, he acted both against his conscience and against his interest, for which he deserved a better requital than this: and yet, perhaps, he would not have been so zealous for the house of Saul if he had not thereby gratified his own ambition and hoped to find his own account in it. Note, Proud men will not bear to be reproved, especially by those whom they think they have obliged. (2.) That he would certainly be revenged on him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.9-2Sam.3.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. With the utmost degree of arrogance and insolence he lets him know that, as he had raised him up, so he could pull him down again and would do it. He knew that God had sworn to David to give him the kingdom, and yet opposed it with all his might from a principle of ambition; but now he complies with it from a principle of revenge, under colour of some regard to the will of God, which was but a pretence. Those that are slaves to their lusts have many masters, which drive, some one way and some another, and, according as they make head, men are violently hurried into self-contradictions. Abner's ambition made him zealous for Ish-bosheth, and now his revenge made him as zealous for David. If he had sincerely regarded God's promise to David, and acted with an eye to that, he would have been steady and uniform in his counsels, and acted in consistency with himself. But, while Abner serves his own lusts, God by him serves his own purposes, makes even his wrath and revenge to praise him, and ordains strength to David by it. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> See how Ish-bosheth was thunder-struck by Abner's insolence: He <hi type="italic">could not answer him again,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.11">v. 11</reference>. If Ish-bosheth had had the spirit of a man, especially of a prince, he might have answered him that his merits were the aggravation of his crimes, that he would not be served by so base a man, and doubted not but to do well enough without him. But he was conscious to himself of his own weakness, and therefore said not a word, lest he should make bad worse. His heart failed him, and he now became, as David had foretold concerning his enemies, like a bowing wall and a <hi type="italic">tottering fence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Ps. lxii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen5996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5997" type="x-p"/> II. Abner treats with David. We must suppose that he began to grow weary of Ish-bosheth's cause, and sought an opportunity to desert it, or else, however he might threaten Ish-bosheth with it, for the quashing of the charge against himself, he would not have made good his angry words so soon as he did, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.12">v. 12</reference>. He <hi type="italic">sent messengers to David,</hi> to tell him that he was at his service. "<hi type="italic">Whose is the land?</hi> Is it not thine? For thou hast the best title to the government and the best interest in the people's affections." Note, God can find out ways to make those serviceable to the kingdom of Christ who yet have no sincere affection for it and who have vigorously set themselves against it. Enemies are sometimes made a footstool, not only to be trodden upon, but to ascend by. The earth helped the woman. <div eID="gen5997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> III. David enters into a treaty with Abner, but upon condition that he shall procure him the restitution of Michal his wife, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.13">v. 13</reference>. Hereby, 1. David showed the sincerity of his conjugal affection to his first and most rightful wife; neither her marrying another, nor his, had alienated him from her. Many waters could not quench that love. 2. He testified his respect to the house of Saul. So far was he from trampling upon it, now that it was fallen, that even in his elevation he valued himself not a little on his relation to it. He cannot be pleased with the honours of the throne unless he have Michal, Saul's daughter, to share with him in them, so far is he from bearing any malice to the family of his enemy. Abner sent him word that he must apply to Ish-bosheth, which he did (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.14">v. 14</reference>), pleading that he had purchased her at a dear rate, and she was wrongfully taken from him. Ish-bosheth durst not deny his demand, now that he had not Abner to stand by him, but took her from Phaltiel, to whom Saul had married her (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.15">v. 15</reference>), and Abner conducted her to David, not doubting but that then he should be doubly welcome when he brought him a wife in one hand and a crown in the other. Her latter husband was loth to part with her, and followed her <hi type="italic">weeping</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.16">v. 16</reference>), but there was no remedy: he must thank himself; for when he took her he knew that another had a right to her. Usurpers must expect to resign. Let no man therefore set his heart on that to which he is not entitled. If any disagreement has separated husband and wife, as they expect the blessing of God let them be reconciled, and come together again; let all former quarrels be forgotten, and let them live together in love, according to God's holy ordinance. <div eID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> IV. Abner uses his interest with the elders of Israel to bring them over to David, knowing that whichever way they went the common people would follow of course. Now that it serves his own turn he can plead in David's behalf that he was, 1. Israel's choice (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You sought for him in times past to be king over you,</hi> when he had signalized himself in so many engagements with the Philistines and done you so much good service; no man can pretend to greater personal merit than David nor to less than Ish-bosheth. You have tried them both, <hi type="italic">Detur digniori—Give the crown to him that best deserves it.</hi> Let David be your king." 2. God's choice (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath spoken of David.</hi> Compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.9">v. 9</reference>. When God appointed Samuel to anoint him he did, in effect, promise that by his hand he would save Israel; for for that end he was made king. God having promised, by David's hand, to save Israel, it is both your duty, in compliance with God's will, and your interest, in order to your victories over your enemies, to submit to him; and it is the greatest folly in the world to oppose him." Who would have expected such reasonings as these out of Abner's mouth? But thus God will make the enemies of his people to know and own <hi type="italic">that he has loved them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. He particularly applied to the men of Benjamin, those of his own tribe, on whom he had the greatest influence, and whom he had drawn in to appear for the house of Saul. He was the man that had deceived them, and therefore he was concerned to undeceive them. Thus the multitude are as they are managed. <div eID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> V. David concludes the treaty with Abner; and he did wisely and well therein; for, whatever induced Abner to it, it was a good work to put an end to the war, and to settle the Lord's anointed on the throne; and it was as lawful for David to make use of his agency as it is for a poor man to receive alms from a Pharisee, who gives it in pride and hypocrisy. Abner reported to David the sense of the people and the success of his communications with them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.19">v. 19</reference>. He came now, not as at first privately, but with a retinue of twenty men, and David entertained them with <hi type="italic">a feast</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.20">v. 20</reference>) in token of reconciliation and joy and as a pledge of the agreement between them: it was a feast upon a covenant, like that, <reference osisRef="Gen.26.30">Gen. xxvi. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">If thy enemy hunger, feed him;</hi> but, if he submit, feast him. Abner, pleased with his entertainment, the prevention of his fall with Saul's house (which would have been inevitable if he had not taken this course), and much more with the prospect he had of preferment under David, undertakes in a little time to perfect the revolution, and to bring all Israel into obedience to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.21">v. 21</reference>. He tells David he shall <hi type="italic">reign over all that his heart desired.</hi> He knew David's elevation took rise from God's appointment, yet he insinuates that it sprang from his own ambition and desire of rule; thus (as bad men often do) he measured that good man by himself. However, David and he parted very good friends, and the affair between them was well settled. Thus it behoves all who fear God and keep his commandments to avoid strife, even with the wicked, to live at peace with all men, and to show the world that they are children of the light.
entries.a60f79b20993fb66e9200aa7c0d7917cd870f323: <div eID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Joab Murders Abner; David's Reflections on Abner's Murder. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1048.)</title> <div sID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, the servants of David and Joab came from <hi type="italic">pursuing</hi> a troop, and brought in a great spoil with them: but Abner <hi type="italic">was</hi> not with David in Hebron; for he had sent him away, and he was gone in peace. <hi type="super">23</hi> When Joab and all the host that <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him were come, they told Joab, saying, Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he hath sent him away, and he is gone in peace. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then Joab came to the king, and said, What hast thou done? behold, Abner came unto thee; why <hi type="italic">is</hi> it <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast sent him away, and he is quite gone? <hi type="super">25</hi> Thou knowest Abner the son of Ner, that he came to deceive thee, and to know thy going out and thy coming in, and to know all that thou doest. <hi type="super">26</hi> And when Joab was come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew <hi type="italic">it</hi> not. <hi type="super">27</hi> And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth <hi type="italic">rib,</hi> that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother. <hi type="super">28</hi> And afterward when David heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> he said, I and my kingdom <hi type="italic">are</hi> guiltless before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for ever from the blood of Abner the son of Ner: <hi type="super">29</hi> Let it rest on the head of Joab, and on all his father's house; and let there not fail from the house of Joab one that hath an issue, or that is a leper, or that leaneth on a staff, or that falleth on the sword, or that lacketh bread. <hi type="super">30</hi> So Joab and Abishai his brother slew Abner, because he had slain their brother Asahel at Gibeon in the battle. <hi type="super">31</hi> And David said to Joab, and to all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner. And king David <hi type="italic">himself</hi> followed the bier. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they buried Abner in Hebron: and the king lifted up his voice, and wept at the grave of Abner; and all the people wept. <hi type="super">33</hi> And the king lamented over Abner, and said, Died Abner as a fool dieth? <hi type="super">34</hi> Thy hands <hi type="italic">were</hi> not bound, nor thy feet put into fetters: as a man falleth before wicked men, <hi type="italic">so</hi> fellest thou. And all the people wept again over him. <hi type="super">35</hi> And when all the people came to cause David to eat meat while it was yet day, David sware, saying, So do God to me, and more also, if I taste bread, or ought else, till the sun be down. <hi type="super">36</hi> And all the people took notice <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> and it pleased them: as whatsoever the king did pleased all the people. <hi type="super">37</hi> For all the people and all Israel understood that day that it was not of the king to slay Abner the son of Ner. <hi type="super">38</hi> And the king said unto his servants, Know ye not that there is a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel? <hi type="super">39</hi> And I <hi type="italic">am</hi> this day weak, though anointed king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah <hi type="italic">be</hi> too hard for me: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness. <div eID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the murder of Abner by Joab, and David's deep resentment of it. <div eID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> I. Joab very insolently fell foul upon David for treating with Abner. He happened to be abroad upon service when Abner was with David, pursuing a troop, either of Philistines or of Saul's party; but, upon his return, he was informed that Abner was just gone (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.22-2Sam.3.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), and that a great many kind things had passed between David and him. He had all the reason in the world to be satisfied of David's prudence and to acquiesce in the measures he took, knowing him to be a wise and good man himself and under a divine conduct in all his affairs; and yet, as if he had the same sway in David's cause that Abner had in Ish-bosheth's, he chides David, and reproaches him to his face as impolitic (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.24-2Sam.3.25">v. 24, 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">What hast thou done?</hi> As if David were accountable to him for what he did: "<hi type="italic">Why hast thou sent him away,</hi> when thou mightest have made him a prisoner? He came as a spy, and will certainly betray thee." I know not whether to wonder more that Joab had impudence enough to give such an affront to his prince or that David had patience enough to take it. He does, in effect, call David <hi type="italic">a fool</hi> when he tells him he knew Abner came to deceive him and yet he trusted him. We find no answer that David gave him, not because he feared him, as Ish-bosheth did Abner (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.11">v. 11</reference>), but because he despised him, or because Joab had not so much good manners as to stay for an answer. <div eID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> II. He very treacherously sent for Abner back, and, under colour of a private conference with him, barbarously killed him with his own hand. That he made use of David's name, under pretence of giving him some further instructions, is intimated in that, <hi type="italic">but David knew it not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.26">v. 26</reference>. Abner, designing no harm, feared none, but very innocently returned to Hebron, and, when he found Joab waiting for him at the gate, turned aside with him to speak with him privately, forgetting what he himself had said when he slew Asahel, <hi type="italic">How shall I hold up my face to Joab thy brother?</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.22">ch. ii. 22</reference>), and there Joab murdered him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.27">v. 27</reference>), and it is intimated (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30">v. 30</reference>) that Abishai was privy to the design, and was aiding and abetting, and would have come in to his brother's assistance if there had been occasion; he is therefore charged as an accessary: <hi type="italic">Joab and Abishai slew Abner,</hi> though perhaps he only knew it who is privy to the thoughts and intents of men's hearts. Now in this, 1. It is certain that the Lord was righteous. Abner had maliciously, and against the convictions of his conscience, opposed David. He had now basely deserted Ish-bosheth, and betrayed him, under pretence of regard to God and Israel, but really from a principle of pride, and revenge, and impatience of control. God will not therefore use so bad a man, though David might, in so good a work as the uniting of Israel. Judgments are prepared for such scorners as Abner was. But, 2. It is as certain that Joab was unrighteous, and, in what he did, did wickedly. David was a man after God's own heart, but could not have those about him, no, not in places of the greatest trust, after his own heart. Many a good prince, and a good master, has been forced to employ bad men. (1.) Even the pretence for doing this was very unjust. Abner had indeed slain his brother Asahel, and Joab and Abishai pretended herein to be the avengers of his blood (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.27">v. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30">30</reference>); but Abner slew Asahel in an open war, wherein Abner indeed had given the challenge, but Joab himself had accepted it and had slain many of Abner's friends. He did it likewise in his own defence, and not till he had given him fair warning (which he would not take), and he did it with reluctancy; but Joab here shed <hi type="italic">the blood of war in peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.5">1 Kings ii. 5</reference>. (2.) That which we have reason to think was at the bottom of Joab's enmity to Abner made it much worse. Joab was now general of David's forces; but, if Abner should come into his interest, he would possibly be preferred before him, being a senior officer, and more experienced in the art of war. This Joab was jealous of, and could better bear the guilt of blood than the thoughts of a rival. (3.) He did it treacherously, and under pretence of speaking peaceably to him, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.24">Deut. xxvii. 24</reference>. Had he challenged him, he would have done like a soldier; but to assassinate him was done villainously and like a coward. <hi type="italic">His words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">Ps. lv. 21</reference>. Thus he basely slew Amasa, <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.9">ch. xx. 9, 10</reference>. (4.) The doing of it was a great affront and injury to David, who was now in treaty with Abner, as Joab knew. Abner was now actually in his master's service, so that, through his side, he struck at David himself. (5.) It was a great aggravation of the murder that he did it in the gate, openly and avowedly, as one that was not ashamed, nor could blush. The gate was the place of judgment and the place of concourse, to that he did it in defiance of justice, both the just sentence of the magistrates and the just resentment of the crowd, as one that neither feared God nor regarded men, but thought himself above all control: and Hebron was a Levites' city and a city of refuge. <div eID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> III. David laid deeply to heart and in many ways expressed his detestation of this execrable villany. <div eID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> 1. He washed his hands from the guilt of Abner's blood. Lest any should suspect that Joab had some secret intimation from David to do as he did (and the rather because he went so long unpunished), he here solemnly appeals to God concerning his innocency: <hi type="italic">I and my kingdom are guiltless</hi> (and my kingdom is so because I am so) <hi type="italic">before the Lord for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.28">v. 28</reference>. It is a comfort to be able to say, when any bad thing is done, that we had no hand in it. <hi type="italic">We have not shed this blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.21.7">Deut. xxi. 7</reference>. However we may be censured or suspected, <hi type="italic">our hearts shall not reproach us.</hi> <div eID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> 2. He entailed the curse for it upon Joab and his family (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">v. 29</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let it rest on the head of Joab.</hi> Let the blood cry against him, and let divine vengeance follow him. Let the iniquity be visited upon his children and children's children, in some hereditary disease or other. The longer the punishment is delayed, the longer let it last when it shall come. Let his posterity be stigmatized, blemished with an issue or a leprosy, which will shut them out from society; let them be beggars, or cripples, or come to some untimely end, that it may be said, He is one of Joab's race." This intimates that the guilt of blood brings a curse upon families; if men do not avenge it, God will, and will lay up the iniquity for the children. But methinks a resolute punishment of the murderer himself would better have become David than this passionate imprecation of God's judgments upon his posterity. <div eID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> 3. He called upon all about him, even Joab himself, to lament the death of Abner (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rend your clothes and mourn before Abner,</hi> that is, before the hearse of Abner, as Abraham is said to mourn <hi type="italic">before his dead</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.2-Gen.23.3">Gen. xxiii. 2, 3</reference>), and he gives a reason why they should attend his funeral with sincere and solemn mourning (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.38">v. 38</reference>), because there is <hi type="italic">a prince and a great man fallen this day in Israel.</hi> His alliance to Saul, his place as general, his interest, and the great services he had formerly done, were enough to denominate him <hi type="italic">a prince and a great man.</hi> When he could not call him a saint or a good man, he said nothing of that, but what was true he gave him the praise of, though he had been his enemy, that he was <hi type="italic">a prince and a great man.</hi> "Such a man has fallen in Israel, and fallen <hi type="italic">this day,</hi> just when he was doing the best deed he ever did in his life, <hi type="italic">this day,</hi> when he was likely to be so serviceable to the public peace and welfare and could so ill be spared." (1.) Let them all lament it. The humbling change death puts all men under is to be lamented, especially as affecting princes and great men. Alas! alas! (see <reference osisRef="Rev.18.10">Rev. xviii. 10</reference>) how mean, how little, are those made by death who made themselves the terror of the mighty in the land of the living! But we are especially obliged to lament the fall of useful men in the midst of their usefulness and when there is most need of them. A public loss must be every man's grief, for every man shares in it. Thus David took care that honour should be done to the memory of a man of merit, to animate others. (2.) Let Joab, in a particular manner, lament it, which he has less heart but more reason to do than any of them. If he could be brought to do it sincerely, it would be an expression of repentance for his sin in slaying him. If he did it in show only, as it is likely he did, yet it was a sort of penance imposed upon him, and a present commutation of the punishment. If he do not as yet expiate the murder with his blood, let him do something towards it with tears. This, perhaps, Joab submitted to with no great reluctancy, now he had gained his point. Now that he is on the bier, no matter in what pomp he lies. <hi type="italic">Sit divus, modo non sit vivus</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let him be canonized, so that he be but killed.</hi> <div eID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> 4. David himself followed the corpse as chief mourner, and made a funeral oration at the grave. He attended the bier (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.31">v. 31</reference>) <hi type="italic">and wept at the grave,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.32">v. 32</reference>. Though Abner had been his enemy, and might possibly have proved no very firm friend, yet because he had been a man of bravery in the field, and might have done great service in the public counsels at this critical juncture, all former quarrels are forgotten and David is a true mourner for his fall. What he said over the grave fetched fresh floods of tears from the eyes of all that were present, when they thought they had already paid the debt in full (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.33-2Sam.3.34">v. 33, 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Died Abner as a fool dieth?</hi> (1.) He speaks as one vexed that Abner was fooled out of his life, that so great a man as he, so famed for conduct and courage, should be imposed upon by a colour of friendship, slain by surprise, and so die as a fool dies. The wisest and stoutest of men have no fence against treachery. To see Abner, who thought himself the main hinge on which the great affairs of Israel turned, so considerable as himself to be able to turn the scale of a trembling government, his head full of great projects and great prospects, to see him made a fool of by a base rival, and falling on a sudden a sacrifice to his ambition and jealousy—this stains the pride of all glory, and should put one out of conceit with worldly grandeur. <hi type="italic">Put not your trust in princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3-Ps.146.4">Ps. cxlvi. 3, 4</reference>. And let us therefore make that sure which we cannot be fooled out of. A man may have his life, and all that is dear to him, taken from him, and not be able to prevent it with all his wisdom, care, and integrity; but there is that which no thief can break through to steal. See here how much more we are beholden to God's providence than to our own prudence for the continuance of our lives and comforts. Were it not for the hold God has of the consciences of bad men, how soon would the weak and innocent become an easy prey to the strong and merciless and the wisest die as fools! Or, (2.) He speaks as one boasting that Abner did not fool himself out of his life: "<hi type="italic">Died Abner as a fool dies?</hi> No, he did not, not as a criminal, a traitor or felon, that forfeits his life into the hands of public justice; his hands were not pinioned, nor his feet fettered, as those of malefactors are: Abner falls not before just men, by a judicial sentence; but as <hi type="italic">a man, an innocent man, falleth before wicked men,</hi> thieves and robbers, so fellest thou." <hi type="italic">Died Abner as Nabal died?</hi> so the LXX. reads it. Nabal died as he lived, like himself, like a sot; but Abner's fate was such as might have been the fate of the wisest and best man in the world. Abner did not throw away his life as Asahel did, who wilfully ran upon the spear, after fair warning, but he was struck by surprise. Note, It is a sad thing to die like a fool, as those do that in any way shorten their own days, and much more those that make no provision for another world. <div eID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6010" type="x-p"/> 5. He fasted all that day, and would by no means be persuaded to eat any thing till night, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.35">v. 35</reference>. It was then the custom of great mourners to refrain for the time from bodily refreshments, as <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.12">ch. i. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.31.13">1 Sam. xxxi. 13</reference>. How incongruous is it then to turn the house of mourning into a house of feasting! This respect which David paid to Abner was very pleasing to the people and satisfied them that he was not, in the least, accessory to the murder (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.36-2Sam.3.37">v. 36, 37</reference>), of which he was solicitous to avoid the suspicion, lest Joab's villany should make him odious, as that of Simeon and Levi did Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Gen. xxxiv. 30</reference>. On this occasion it is said, <hi type="italic">Whatever the king did pleased all the people.</hi> This intimates, (1.) His good affection to them. He studied to please them in every thing and carefully avoided what might be disobliging. (2.) Their good opinion of him. They thought every thing he did well done. Such a mutual willingness to please, and easiness to be pleased, will make every relation comfortable. <div eID="gen6010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6011" type="x-p"/> 6. He bewailed it that he could not with safety do justice on the murderers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30">v. 30</reference>. He was weak, his kingdom was newly planted, and a little shake would overthrow it. Joab's family had a great interest, were bold and daring, and to make them his enemies now might be of bad consequence. These sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him, too big for the law to take hold of; and therefore, though by man, by the magistrate, the blood of a murderer <hi type="italic">should be shed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen. ix. 6</reference>), David bears the sword in vain, and contents himself, as a private person, to leave them to the judgment of God: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall reward the doer of evil according to his wickedness.</hi> Now this is a diminution, (1.) To David's greatness. He is anointed king, and yet is kept in awe by his own subjects, and some of them are too hard for him. Who would be fond of power when a man may have the name of it, and must be accountable for it, and yet be hampered in the use of it? (2.) To David's goodness. He ought to have done his duty, and trusted God with the issue. <hi type="italic">Fiat justitia, ruat coelum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let justice be done, though the heavens should fall asunder.</hi> If the law had had its course against Joab, perhaps the murder of Ishbosheth, Amnon, and others, would have been prevented. It was carnal policy and cruel pity that spared Joab. Righteousness supports the throne and will never shake it. Yet it was only a reprieve that David gave to Joab; on his death-bed he left it to Solomon (who could the better wield the sword of justice because he had no occasion to draw the sword of war) to avenge the blood of Abner. Evil pursues sinners, and will overtake them at last. David preferred Abner's son Jaasiel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.21">1 Chron. xxvii. 21</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Sam.3"/> <div eID="gen6011" type="x-p"/>

entries.4bb7302787d0c414dfb61726a3e63b345f1d637d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2840"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1-2Sam.3.5">2Sa 3:1-5</reference>. Six Sons Born to David.<div eID="gen3907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2840"/><hi type="bold">1. there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David--</hi>The rival parties had varying success, but David's interest steadily increased; less, however, by the fortunes of war, than a growing adherence to him as the divinely designated king. <div eID="gen3908" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b6504b9ebaf350cb65511b224779afb1ae54dc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2841"/><div sID="gen3909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2841"/><hi type="bold">2. unto David were sons born in Hebron--</hi>The six sons mentioned had all different mothers. <div eID="gen3909" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bf1003d3cb150acbd9fa82702ad6ca10c35f1bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2842"/><div sID="gen3910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2842"/><hi type="bold">3. Chileab--</hi>("his father's picture")--called also Daniel (<reference osisRef="1Chr.3.1">1Ch 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen3910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur--</hi>a region in Syria, north of Israel. This marriage seems to have been a political match, made by David, with a view to strengthen himself against Ish-bosheth's party, by the aid of a powerful friend and ally in the north. Piety was made to yield to policy, and the bitter fruits of this alliance with a heathen prince he reaped in the life of the turbulent Absalom. <div eID="gen3911" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b3060a16e262d098e95673b7357a0a649f60b76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2843"/><div sID="gen3912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2843"/><hi type="bold">5. Eglah David's wife--</hi>This addition has led many to think that Eglah was another name for Michal, the first and proper wife, who, though she had no family after her insolent ridicule of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.23">2Sa 6:23</reference>), might have had a child before.<div eID="gen3912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3913" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6-2Sam.3.12">2Sa 3:6-12</reference>. Abner Revolts to David. <div eID="gen3913" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9c4df5869985619774761831bb6bcbce0ac9e4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2844"/><div sID="gen3914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2844"/><hi type="bold">6-11. Abner made himself strong for the house of Saul--</hi>In the East, the wives and concubines of a king are the property of his successor to this extent, that for a private person to aspire to marry one of them would be considered a virtual advance of pretensions to the crown (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.17">1Ki 2:17</reference>). It is not clear whether the accusation against Abner was well or ill founded. But he resented the charge as an indignity, and, impelled by revenge, determined to transfer all the weight of his influence to the opposite party. He evidently set a full value on his services, and seems to have lorded it over his weak nephew in a haughty, overbearing manner. <div eID="gen3914" type="x-p"/>
entries.436fdd1cdaaee8d37ab825e89090311576db1f7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2845"/><div sID="gen3915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2845"/><hi type="bold">12-13. Abner sent messengers to David--</hi>Though his language implied a secret conviction, that in supporting Ish-bosheth he had been laboring to frustrate the divine purpose of conferring the sovereignty of the kingdom on David, this acknowledgment was no justification either of the measure he was now adopting, or of the motives that prompted it. Nor does it seem possible to uphold the full integrity and honor of David's conduct in entertaining his secret overtures for undermining Ish-bosheth, except we take into account the divine promise of the kingdom, and his belief that the secession of Abner was a means designed by Providence for accomplishing it. The demand for the restoration of his wife Michal was perfectly fair; but David's insisting on it at that particular moment, as an indispensable condition of his entering into any treaty with Abner, seems to have proceeded not so much from a lingering attachment as from an expectation that his possession of her would incline some adherents of the house of Saul to be favorable to his cause. <div eID="gen3915" type="x-p"/>
entries.50a9deaacb6c2e1af68ce26fc8abbb5262991a82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2846"/><div sID="gen3916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2846"/><hi type="bold">17-21. Abner had communication with the elders of Israel--</hi>He spoke the truth in impressing their minds with the well-known fact of David's divine designation to the kingdom. But he acted a base and hypocritical part in pretending that his present movement was prompted by religious motives, when it sprang entirely from malice and revenge against Ish-bosheth. The particular appeal of the Benjamites was a necessary policy; their tribe enjoyed the honor of giving birth to the royal dynasty of Saul; they would naturally be disinclined to lose that prestige. They were, besides, a determined people, whose contiguity to Judah might render them troublesome and dangerous. The enlistment of their interest, therefore, in the scheme, would smooth the way for the adhesion of the other tribes; and Abner enjoyed the most convenient opportunity of using his great influence in gaining over that tribe while escorting Michal to David with a suitable equipage. The mission enabled him to cover his treacherous designs against his master--to draw the attention of the elders and people to David as uniting in himself the double recommendation of being the nominee of Jehovah, no less than a connection of the royal house of Saul, and, without suspicion of any dishonorable motives, to advocate policy of terminating the civil discord, by bestowing the sovereignty on the husband of Michal. In the same character of public ambassador, he was received and feted by David; and while, ostensibly, the restoration of Michal was the sole object of his visit, he busily employed himself in making private overtures to David for bringing over to his cause those tribes which he had artfully seduced. Abner pursued a course unworthy of an honorable man and though his offer was accepted by David, the guilt and infamy of the transaction were exclusively his.<div eID="gen3916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3917" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.22-2Sam.3.30">2Sa 3:22-30</reference>. Joab Kills Abner. <div eID="gen3917" type="x-p"/>
entries.49dbfa6beae5deb54d22be3ca6649b9695250060: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2847"/><div sID="gen3918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2847"/><hi type="bold">24-27. Joab came to the king, and said, What hast thou done?--</hi>Joab's knowledge of Abner's wily character might have led him to doubt the sincerity of that person's proposals and to disapprove the policy of relying on his fidelity. But undoubtedly there were other reasons of a private and personal nature which made Joab displeased and alarmed by the reception given to Abner. The military talents of that general, his popularity with the army, his influence throughout the nation, rendered him a formidable rival. In the event of his overtures being carried out, the important service of bringing over all the other tribes to the king of Judah would establish so strong a claim on the gratitude of David, that his accession would inevitably raise a serious obstacle to the ambition of Joab. To these considerations was added the remembrance of the blood feud that existed between them since the death of his brother Asahel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.23">2Sa 2:23</reference>). Determined, therefore, to get Abner out of the way, Joab feigned some reason, probably in the king's name, for recalling him, and, going out to meet him, stabbed him unawares; not within Hebron, for it was a city of refuge, but at a noted well in the neighborhood. <div eID="gen3918" type="x-p"/>
entries.e706a15d5f994af26c13ea95178facf94cdb874d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2848"/><div sID="gen3919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2848"/><hi type="bold">31. David said to Joab, and to all the people that were with him, Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth--</hi>David's sorrow was sincere and profound, and he took occasion to give it public expression by the funeral honors he appointed for Abner.<div eID="gen3919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">King David himself followed the bier--</hi>a sort of wooden frame, partly resembling a coffin, and partly a hand-barrow. <div eID="gen3920" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb50029c6e4cce0b4228fc86e50b7804ac442e74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2849"/><div sID="gen3921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2849"/><hi type="bold">33-34. the king lamented over Abner--</hi>This brief elegy is an effusion of indignation as much as of sorrow. As Abner had stabbed Asahel in open war [2Sa 2:23], Joab had not the right of the Goel. Besides, he had adopted a lawless and execrable method of obtaining satisfaction (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.5">1Ki 2:5</reference>). The deed was an insult to the authority, as well as most damaging to the prospects of the king. But David's feelings and conduct on hearing of the death, together with the whole character and accompaniments of the funeral solemnity, tended not only to remove all suspicion of guilt from him, but even to turn the tide of popular opinion in his favor, and to pave the way for his reigning over all the tribes more honorably than by the treacherous negotiations of Abner. <chapter eID="2Sam.3"/>

entries.f9c3e3b8087f3643a6a8414276d62ef320b5eef0: <div eID="gen10732" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10733" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10734" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10734" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10733" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10735" type="x-p"/> Account of the children born to David in Hebron, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1-2Sam.3.5">2Sam 3:1-5</reference>. Abner being accused by Ish-bosheth of familiarities with Rizpah, Saul's concubine, he is enraged; offers his services to David; goes to Hebron, and makes a league with him, vv. 6-22. Joab, through enmity to Abner, pretends to David that he came as a spy, and should not be permitted to return, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.23-2Sam.3.25">2Sam 3:23-25</reference>. He follows Abner, and treacherously slays him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.26">2Sam 3:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.27">2Sam 3:27</reference>. David hearing of it is greatly incensed against Joab, and pronounces a curse upon him and upon his family, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.28">2Sam 3:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.29">2Sam 3:29</reference>. He commands a general mourning for Abner, and himself follows the bier weeping, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.30-2Sam.3.32">2Sam 3:30-32</reference>. David's lamentation over Abner, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.33">2Sam 3:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.34">2Sam 3:34</reference>. The people solicit David to take meat; but he fasts the whole day, and complains to them of the insolence and intrigues of Joab and his brothers: the people are pleased with his conduct, <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.35-2Sam.3.39">2Sam 3:35-39</reference>. <div eID="gen10735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> There was long war - Frequent battles and skirmishes took place between the followers of David and the followers of Ish-bosheth, after the two years mentioned above, to the end of the fifth year, in which Ish-bosheth was slain by Rechab and Baanah.
entries.9ad58d44347c18bae15d2e7efab220d546f74648: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> Abner made himself strong - This strengthening of himself, and going in to the late king's concubine, were most evident proofs that he wished to seize upon the government. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.21">1Kgs 2:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.22">1Kgs 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.8">1Kgs 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.21">1Kgs 16:21</reference>.
entries.b7d574e222f3a869afcfac0b51aaf31817f2f779: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> Am I a dog's head - Dost thou treat a man with indignity who has been the only prop of thy tottering kingdom, and the only person who could make head against the house of David?
entries.04caca78f0b8d449c8781485dfa1ca9d90ede8a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> Except, as the Lord hath sworn to David - And why did he not do this before, when he knew that God had given the kingdom to David? Was he not now, according to his own concession, fighting against God?
entries.63dc2de97ac5754232ced417fabe11f9df037243: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> He could not answer Abner a word - Miserable is the lot of a king who is governed by the general of his army, who may strip him of his power and dignity whenever he pleases! Witness the fate of poor Charles I. of England and Louis XVI. of France. Military men, above all others, should never be intrusted with any civil power, and should be great only in the field.
entries.e8d69c609647a239c4aa4c8f197efa00e148e5b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> Except thou first bring Michal - David had already six wives at Hebron; and none of them could have such pretensions to legitimacy as Michal, who had been taken away from him and married to Phaltiel. However distressing it was to take her from a husband who loved her most tenderly, (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.16">2Sam 3:16</reference>), yet prudence and policy required that he should strengthen his own interest in the kingdom as much as possible; and that he should not leave a princess in the possession of a man who might, in her right, have made pretensions to the throne. Besides, she was his own lawful wife, and he had a right to demand her when he pleased.
entries.d81670370dfa887fda48c74d65d7c21e8c6ab3a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> Deliver me my wife - It is supposed that he meant to screen Abner; and to prevent that violence which he might have used in carrying off Michal.
entries.8b7998dec2cbced5598f50d95bf019b8ab201f0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> Weeping behind her - If genuine affection did not still subsist between David and Michal, it was a pity to have taken her from Phaltiel, who had her to wife from the conjoint authority of her father and her king. <div eID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless David had a legal right to her, as she had never been divorced, for she was taken from him by the hand of violence.
entries.3839c78ae62c56b0292d43d3382838091446d256: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath spoken of David - Where is this spoken? Such a promise is not extant. Perhaps it means no more than, "Thus, it may be presumed, God hath determined."
entries.ddbaeb57e97e23938132a6a40383064e7411be91: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10747" type="x-p"/> He went in peace - David dismissed him in good faith, having no sinister design in reference to him.
entries.4606d79eff51d664526f5f43dd48a7eacf2da38a: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen10747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10748" type="x-p"/> And smote him there - Joab feared that, after having rendered such essential services to David, Abner would be made captain of the host: he therefore determined to prevent it by murdering the man, under pretense of avenging the death of his brother Asahel. <div eID="gen10748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10749" type="x-p"/> The murder, however, was one of the most unprovoked and wicked: and such was the power and influence of this nefarious general, that the king dared not to bring him to justice for his crime. In the same way he murdered Amasa, a little time afterwards. See <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.10">2Sam 20:10</reference>. Joab was a cool-blooded, finished murderer. "Treason and murder ever keep together, like two yoke-devils."
entries.3ee609eb1fa4c6c07ca761eac2555176317bccf9: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen10749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10750" type="x-p"/> Let it rest on the head - All these verbs may be rendered in the future tense: it will rest on the head of Joab, etc. This was a prophetic declaration, which sufficiently showed the displeasure of God against this execrable man.
entries.fffa09f760d8e9d201510b3cee2fbd219dc2a899: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen10750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> David said to Joab - He commanded him to take on him the part of a principal mourner.
entries.f837b73b5f96f659e5691c312725114e1c48f4ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10752" type="x-p"/> The king lamented over Abner - This lamentation, though short, is very pathetic. It is a high strain of poetry; but the measure cannot be easily ascertained. Our own translation may be measured thus: - <div eID="gen10752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10753" type="x-p"/> Died Abner as a fool dieth? <div eID="gen10753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10754" type="x-p"/> Thy hands were not bound, <div eID="gen10754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10755" type="x-p"/> Nor thy feet put into fetters. <div eID="gen10755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10756" type="x-p"/> As a man falleth before the wicked. <div eID="gen10756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> So hast thou fallen! <div eID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> Or thus: - <div eID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10759" type="x-p"/> Shall Abner die a death like to a villain's? <div eID="gen10759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> Thy hands not bound, <div eID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10761" type="x-p"/> Nor were the fetters to thy feet applied. <div eID="gen10761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10762" type="x-p"/> Like as one falls before the sons of guilt, <div eID="gen10762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> So hast thou fallen! <div eID="gen10763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10764" type="x-p"/> He was not taken away by the hand of justice, nor in battle, nor by accident: he died the death of a culprit by falling into the hands of a villain. <div eID="gen10764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> This song was a heavy reproof to Joab; and must have galled him extremely, being sung by all the people.
entries.8d8ff33e4756b29619c7cad7d812b36bd33746ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen10765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> The people took notice - They saw that the king's grief was sincere, and that he had no part nor device in the murder of Abner: see <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.37">2Sam 3:37</reference>.
entries.2cafbbc62c72a943e6a62243e2cb4a9511149dcc: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen10766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> I am this day weak - Had Abner lived, all the tribes of Israel would have been brought under my government. <div eID="gen10767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> Though anointed king - I have little else than the title: first, having only one tribe under my government; and secondly, the sons of Zeruiah, Joab and his brethren, having usurped all the power, and reduced me to the shadow of royalty. <div eID="gen10768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall reward the doer of evil - That is, Joab, whom he appears afraid to name. <div eID="gen10769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10770" type="x-p"/> We talk much of ancient manners, their simplicity and ingenuousness; and say that the former days were better than these. But who says this who is a judge of the times? In those days of celebrated simplicity, etc., there were not so many crimes as at present I grant: but what they wanted in number they made up in degree: deceit, cruelty, rapine, murder, and wrong of almost every kind, then flourished. We are refined in our vices; they were gross and barbarous in theirs: they had neither so many ways nor so many means of sinning; but the sum of their moral turpitude was greater than ours. We have a sort of decency and good breeding, which lay a certain restraint on our passions, they were boorish and beastly, and their bad passions were ever in full play. Civilization prevents barbarity and atrocity; mental cultivation induces decency of manners: those primitive times were generally without these. Who that knows them would wish such ages to return?  <chapter eID="2Sam.3"/> <div eID="gen10770" type="x-p"/>

entries.875f165de6cc0871e6d87b5c172da57259e3ea9d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.1">2Sa 3:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“And the war became long</hi> (was protracted)<hi type="italic">between the house of Saul and the house of David; but David became stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul weaker and weaker.”</hi> הלך, when connected with another verb or with an adjective, expresses the idea of the gradual progress of an affair (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> §131, 3, Anm. 3). The historian sums up in these words the historical course of the two royal houses, as they stood opposed to one another. <hi type="italic">“The war”</hi> does not mean continual fighting, but the state of hostility or war in which they continued to stand towards one another. They concluded no peace, so that David was not recognised by Ishbosheth as king, any more than Ishbosheth by David. Not only is there nothing said about any continuance of actual warfare by Abner or Ishbosheth after the loss of the battle at Gibeon, but such a thing was very improbable in itself, as Ishbosheth was too weak to be able to carry on the war, whilst David waited with firm reliance upon the promise of the Lord, until all Israel should come over to him.
entries.7a5e512d742cbf9f841b6f120d1d47a84e21d575: <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.2-2Sam.3.5">2Sa 3:2-5</reference> <div eID="gen4256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4257" type="x-p"/> Growth of the House of David. - Proof of the advance of the house of David is furnished by the multiplication of his family at Hebron. The account of the <hi type="italic">sons who were born to David at Hebron</hi> does not break the thread, as Clericus, Thenius, and others suppose, but is very appropriately introduced here, as a practical proof of the strengthening of the house of David, in harmony with the custom of beginning the history of the reign of every king with certain notices concerning his family (vid., 2Sa 5:13.; 1Ki 3:1; 1Ki 14:21; 1Ki 15:2, 1Ki 15:9, etc.). We have a similar list of the sons of David in <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.1">1Ch 3:1</reference>-4. The first two sons were born to him from the two wives whom he had brought with him to Hebron (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.42-1Sam.25.43">1Sa 25:42-43</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> וילדו is probably only a copyist’s error for ויּוּלדוּ, which is the reading in many Codices. From <hi type="italic">Ahinoam</hi> - the first-born, <hi type="italic">Amnon</hi> (called Aminon in <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.20">2Sa 13:20</reference>); from Abigail - the second, <hi type="italic">Chileab</hi>. The latter is also called <hi type="italic">Daniel</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.1">1Ch 3:1</reference>, and therefore had probably two names. The <hi type="italic">lamed</hi> before Ahinoam and the following names serves as a periphrasis for the genitive, like the German <hi type="italic">von</hi>, in consequence of the word <hi type="italic">son</hi> being omitted (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §292, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). The other four were by wives whom he had married in Hebron: <hi type="italic">Absalom</hi> by <hi type="italic">Maachah</hi>, the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, a small kingdom in the north-east of Bashan (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>); <hi type="italic">Adonijah</hi> by <hi type="italic">Haggith</hi>; <hi type="italic">Shephatiah</hi> by <hi type="italic">Abital</hi>; and <hi type="italic">Ithream</hi> by <hi type="italic">Eglah</hi>. The origin of the last three wives is unknown. The clause appended to Eglah’s name, viz., <hi type="italic">“David’s wife,”</hi> merely serves as a fitting conclusion to the whole list (Bertheau on <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.3">1Ch 3:3</reference>), and is not added to show that Eglah was David’s principal wife, which would necessitate the conclusion drawn by the Rabbins, that Michal was the wife intended.
entries.ab3f315fb75d52bc03b7e09325d06e9fa276aea9: <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6-2Sam.3.39">2Sa 3:6-39</reference> <div eID="gen4257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4258" type="x-p"/> Decline of the House of Saul. - <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6">2Sa 3:6</reference>-11. <hi type="italic">Abner’s quarrel with Ishbosheth.</hi> -  During the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner adhered firmly to the house of Saul, but he appropriated one of Saul’s concubines to himself. When Ishbosheth charged him with this, he fell into so violent a rage, that he at once announced to Ishbosheth his intention to hand over the kingdom to David. Abner had certainly perceived the utter incapacity of Ishbosheth for a very long time, if not from the very outset, and had probably made him king after the death of Saul, merely that he might save himself from the necessity of submitting to David, and might be able to rule in Ishbosheth’s name, and possibly succeed in paving his own way to the throne. His appropriation of the concubine of the deceased monarch was at any rate a proof, according to Israelitish notions, and in fact those generally prevalent in the East, that he was aiming at the throne (vid., <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.21">2Sa 16:21</reference>; 1Ki 2:21). But it may gradually have become obvious to him, that the house of Saul could not possibly retain the government in opposition to David; and this may have led to his determination to persuade all the Israelites to acknowledge David, and thereby to secure for himself an influential post under his government. This will explain in a very simple manner Abner’s falling away from Ishbosheth and going over to David.  <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6-2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:6-7</reference> <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.6">2Sa 3:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:7</reference> constitute one period, expanded by the introduction of circumstantial clauses, the ויהי (it came to pass) of the protasis being continued in the ויּאמר (he said) of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:7</reference></hi>. <hi type="italic">“It came to pass, when there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, and Abner showed himself strong for the house of Saul, and Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, that he</hi> (Ishbosheth) <hi type="italic">said to Abner, Why hast thou gone to my father’s concubine?”</hi> The subject to <hi type="italic">“said”</hi> is omitted in the apodosis; but it is evident from <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.8">2Sa 3:8</reference>, and the expression <hi type="italic">“my father,”</hi> that Ishbosheth is to be supplied. Even in the second circumstantial clause, <hi type="italic">“and Saul had a concubine,”</hi> the reason why this is mentioned is only to be gathered from Ishbosheth’s words. בּ התחזק: to prove one’s self strong for, or with, a person, i.e., to render him powerful help. אל בּוא means <hi type="italic">“to cohabit with.”</hi> It was the exclusive right of the successor to the throne to cohabit with the concubines of the deceased king, who came down to him as part of the property which he inherited.

And <ns0:hi>a Dogs head</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>a Dog</ns0:hi> by a Synecdoche, usual both in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> and in other Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guages, as the <ns0:hi>Head</ns0:hi> is oft put for the whole <ns0:hi>Man</ns0:hi> in the <ns0:hi>La<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tin</ns0:hi> Tongue.</ns0:note>, which against <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">So the Particle <ns0:hi>Lamed</ns0:hi> is well rendred, as <ns0:hi>el,</ns0:hi> which among the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> is confessedly of the same na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture and use, is used <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 9. 14. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 34. 7. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 13. 9, 20. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 7. 15.</ns0:note> Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father, to his brethren, and to his friends, and have not delivered thee into the hand of David <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which I could oft and easily have done.</ns0:note>, that thou chargest me to day with a fault concerning this woman <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either that thou accusest me falsly concerning this matter: or, that thou canst not wink at so small a fault (for so he esteemed it) as conversation with this Woman, who, what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever she formerly was, is now so impotent and inconsider<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />able, that she can do thee no service, as I have done.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
