                  <ns0:p n="12">12 ¶ And Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Who in his name and stead might treat with <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> concerning his Reconciliation with him. Thus God over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rules the Lusts and Passions of wicked Men, to accomplish his own Wise and Holy purposes. And who then dare con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend with that God who makes even his Enemies to do his work, and destroy themselves?</ns0:note>, saying, Whose <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the land <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To whom doth this whole Land belong, but to thee? Is it not thine by Divine right? <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Son is but an Usurper, thou onely art the rightful owner.</ns0:note>? saying <ns0:hi>also,</ns0:hi> Make thy league with me <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">That thou wiltst pardon all past offences to me, and to all <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and thou wiltst receive me into thy grace and favour.</ns0:note>, and behold, my hand <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> with thee, to bring about all Israel unto thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 ¶ And he said, Well, I will make a league with thee <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, upon thy terms: which, all circumstances con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sidered, seems to be lawful, to prevent the great effusion of <ns0:hi>Israelitish</ns0:hi> Blood, which otherwise would certainly have been spilt. And although the principle of this action of <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi>'s was base and wicked, yet the action it self was Lawful and Commendable, and no more than his Duty to God and <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> obliged him to; and therefore <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might well per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />suade and induce him to it.</ns0:note>: but one thing I require of thee, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> saying.</ns0:note> that is, Thou shalt not see my face, except thou first bring Michal Sauls daughter, when thou comest to see my face.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth Sauls son <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Whose consent was necessary, both to take her away from her present Husband, and to persuade her to return to <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi> Hereby also <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> opened to him also a door of hope for his Reconciliation, lest being desperate he should hinder <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi> in his present design.</ns0:note>, saying, Deliver <ns0:hi>me</ns0:hi> my wife Michal <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Who, though she was taken from me by force, and constrained to marry another, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25. 44. yet is indeed my rightful Wife. Her <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> demands, partly, for the affection he formerly had, and still retained to her: partly, to deliver her from the sin and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proach of Adultery with another Man, who was not in truth and justice her Husband, though he was so called and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted: and partly, upon a politick consideration, that she might strengthen his Right and Title to the Kingdom.</ns0:note>, which I espoused to me <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 18. 25, 27.</ns0:note> for an hundred fore-skins of the Philistines.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Ish-bosheth sent and took her from <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> husband <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For, being forsaken by <ns0:hi>Abner,</ns0:hi> he durst not deny <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> into whose power he saw he must unavoidably come: and besides, he supposed that she might be an effectual instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment to make his peace with <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> from <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 25. 44. <ns0:hi>Phalt<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Phaltiel the son of Laish.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And her husband went with her <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> going and weeping.</ns0:note> along weeping behind her to Bahurim <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">A City of <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> upon the Borders of <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi> See 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 16. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 8.</ns0:note>: then said Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner unto him, Go, return. And he returned.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 ¶ And Abner had communication with the elders of Israel, saying, Ye sought for David <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> both yesterday and the third <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> in times past <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> king over you <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Even in <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s time you highly honoured him, and prized his conduct, and wished that the power were in his hands; and great numbers of you went to him, when he was in the Hold, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 12. And after <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s death you would glad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly have advanced him to the Crown, if your respect to <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Family, together with my Authority and Influence, had not diverted you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Now then do <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">You shall have my free consent and utmost assistance in procuring it.</ns0:note>; for the LORD hath spoken of David <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He wickedly pretends Religion, when he intended nothing but the satisfaction of his own pride, and malice, and fury, against <ns0:hi>Ishbosheth.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, saying, By the hand of my ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant David, I will save my people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines, and out of the hand of all their enemies <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It is very probable God spake these words, but undoubtedly he spake the same sense by <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> though it be not expressed before.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And Abner also spake in the ears of Benja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To these he particularly applies himself, because they might be thought most kind to <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and his House, and most loth to let the Kingdom go out of their own Tribe; and therefore it was necessary that he should use all his art and power with them, to persuade them to a compliance with his design; and besides, they were a Valiant Tribe, and bor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dering upon <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and situate between them and the other Tribes; and therefore the winning of them, would be of mighty concernment to bring in all the rest.</ns0:note>: and Abner went also to speak in the ears of David in Hebron, all that seemed good to Isra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />el, and that seemed good to the whole house of Benjamin.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 So Abner came to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him: and David made Abner, and the men that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, a feast <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which in those times was customary when Persons en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tred into Covenant. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 30. and 31. 44, 46.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And Abner said unto David, I will arise, and go, and will gather all Israel <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Elders and Chieftains of all <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> Represent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing and Ruling all the rest.</ns0:note> unto my lord the king, that they may make a league with thee, and that thou mayest reign over all that thy heart de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sireth. And David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 ¶ And behold, the servants of David, and Joab, came from <ns0:hi>pursuing</ns0:hi> a troop <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Of Robbers, either <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Edomites,</ns0:hi> or some others, who taking advantage of the discord between the Houses of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> made inroads into <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> as they had occasion.</ns0:note>, and brought in a great spoil with them: (but Abner <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> not with David in Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he was gone in peace).</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:249" />23 When Joab and all the host that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> with him, were come, they told Joab, saying, Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he hath sent him away, and he is gone in peace.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Then Joab came to the king, and said, What hast thou done <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Thou hast committed a great oversight, to dismiss so dangerous and mischievous a Person, when he was in thy hands.</ns0:note>? behold, Abner came unto thee: why <ns0:hi>is it</ns0:hi> that thou hast sent him away, and he is quite gone?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Thou knowest Abner the son of Ner, that he came to deceive thee, and to know thy going out, and thy coming in <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To search out thy counsels and secret designs, and to make use of them against thee.</ns0:note>, and to know all that thou dost.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And when Joab was come out from David, he sent messengers after Abner <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">In the Kings name, and upon pretence of some further communication with him.</ns0:note>, which brought him again from the well of Sirah: but David knew <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 King. 2. 5.</ns0:note> took him aside in the gate <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In the entrance into the City before he came to the King; and in the place where conferences used to be.</ns0:note>, to speak with him <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> peacea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly.</ns0:note> quietly <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">With appearance of great civility and kindness. Or, <ns0:hi>se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cretly,</ns0:hi> as having some matter of great importance to utter, which none but himself must hear.</ns0:note>: and smote him there under the fifth <ns0:hi>rib</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As he did <ns0:hi>Asahel, chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 23.</ns0:note>, that he died, for the blood of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2. 23.</ns0:note> Asahel his brother <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To revenge the death of <ns0:hi>Asahel;</ns0:hi> and withal (though that be not here mentioned to secure his own stand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, and rid his hands of so great and powerful a Competitor. And this was <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s design; but God had other designs in it, both to punish <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi>'s manifold wickedness, and particular<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly his rebellion against <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and against God and his own Conscience therein: and that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might not owe his Kingdom to <ns0:hi>Abner,</ns0:hi> and to his revenge and treachery, but wholly to Gods Wise and Powerful Providence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 ¶ And afterward when David heard it, he said <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Publickly before his Courtiers and People; and serious<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly as in Gods presence.</ns0:note>, I and my kingdom <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> guiltless before the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">I call the Lord to Witness, that this was not done by my Instigation or Authority, or by any publick Counsel, but onely by <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s malice; and therefore I trust that God will not punish me nor my Kingdom, but <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> onely.</ns0:note> for ever, from the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> bloods.</ns0:note> blood of Abner the son of Ner:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Let it <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> This Blood, the guilt and punishment of it.</ns0:note> rest on the head of Joab, and on all his fathers house <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">But Children were not to suffer for their Parents sin, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24. 16. And therefore either this was onely a Prediction; or, if it were an Imprecation, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> may seem to have transgressed his bounds, and mingled his Passion with his Zeal, that so he might express his utter detestation of this horrid Murder, and how far he was from having any hand in it.</ns0:note>, and let there not <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> be cut off.</ns0:note> fail from the house of Joab one that hath an issue <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which was not onely a troublesome and shameful Diseases, but also infe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctious, both to him that had it, and to all that touched him: so that, whilst it was upon a man, he was cut off in a great part from converse either with God or men.</ns0:note>, or that is a leper, or that leaneth on a staff <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Through craziness, or feebleness, or lameness, whereby he he is ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dred unfit for action and publick service.</ns0:note>, or that fal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />leth on the sword, or that lacketh bread.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 So Joab and Abishai <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For though <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> onely committed the Murder, yet <ns0:hi>Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shai</ns0:hi> was guilty of it, because it was done with his consent, and counsel, and help, and approbation: for by these and such like actions men are involved in the guilt of other mens sins, at least in Gods judgment.</ns0:note> his brother slew Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner, because he had slain their brother <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2. 23.</ns0:note> Asahel at Gibeon in the battel <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which he did in the fury of Battel, and for his own necessary defence; and therefore it was no justification of this unnecessary and treacherous Murder in a time of peace.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 ¶ And David said to Joab <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Him he especially obliged to it; partly, to bring him to Repentance for his sin: partly, to expose him to publick shame, and to the contempt and hatred of all the people, with whom he had too great an interest, which hereby <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> designed to diminish.</ns0:note>, and to all the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 7. 6.</ns0:note> Rent your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Attending upon his Corps, and paying him that respect and honour which was due to his quality.</ns0:note>. And king David <ns0:hi>himself</ns0:hi> followed the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> bed.</ns0:note> bier <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which was against the usage of Kings, and might seem below <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Dignity; but it was now expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dient to vindicate himself from all suspition of contrivance or concurrence in this action.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And they buried Abner in Hebron, and the king list up his voice, and wept at the grave of Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner, and all the pleople wept.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And the king lamented over Abner, and said, Died Abner as † a fool dieth?<ns0:note place="margin">‡ <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>b i. e.</ns0:hi> As a wicked man, for such are oft called <ns0:hi>Fools</ns0:hi> in Scripture. Was he cut off by the hands of Justice for his crimes? Nothing less; but by <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s malice and treachery. Or, did he die by his own folly, because he had not Wisdom or courage to defend himself? Ah no. The words may be thus rendred: <ns0:hi>shall</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>should</ns0:hi> Abner <ns0:hi>die like a Fool,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a vile contemptible Person? i. e.</ns0:hi> unregarded, unpitied, unrevenged; as Fools or vile Persons die, for whose death none are con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerned. Or, <ns0:hi>How is</ns0:hi> Abner <ns0:hi>dead like a Fool!</ns0:hi> pitying his mischance. It being honourable for a great Man and a Sol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dier to fight, if met with an Enemy, and not (having his Arms at liberty) stand still like a Fool to be killed, without making any resistance or defence; which, by this treachery of <ns0:hi>Ioab,</ns0:hi> happened to be his case.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 Thy hands <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> not bound, nor thy feet put into setters <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Thou didst not tamely yield up thy self to <ns0:hi>Ioab,</ns0:hi> as his Prisoner, to be bound hand and foot at his pleasure. <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> did not overcome thee generously and honourably in an equal Combat, nor durst he attempt thee in that way, as a General or Soldier of any worth would have done.</ns0:note>: as a man falleth before <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> children in iniquity.</ns0:note> wicked men <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>before,</ns0:hi> i. e. in the presence, or by the hands of <ns0:hi>froward,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>perverse,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>crooked men,</ns0:hi> by Hypocrisie and Perfidiousness, whereby the vilest Coward may kill the most Valiant person. Thus he reproached <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> to his very face, before all the people: which was a great Evidence of his own In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nocency herein; because otherwise <ns0:hi>Ioab,</ns0:hi> being so power<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, and proud, and petulant to his Sovereign, would never have taken the shame and blame of it wholly to himself, as he did.</ns0:note>, so fellest thou. And all the people wept a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gain over him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 And when all the people came to cause Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid to eat meat <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Till evening, for then Fasting Days ended of course.</ns0:note>, while it was yet day, David sware, saying, So do God to me, and more also, if I taste bread, or ought else, till the sun be down <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Till evening, for then Fasting Days ended of course.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>d</ns0:hi> To refresh and chear up his depressed Spirits; as they used to do at Funerals<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> See <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 16. 5. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 24. 17.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 And all the people too notice <ns0:hi>of it,</ns0:hi> and it <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> was good in the<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r eyes.</ns0:note> pleased them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">They were satisfied concerning <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Integrity, and the method he used here for his own just vindication.</ns0:note>: as whatsoever the king did <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either in this matter: or rather, in all things following this Action. The meaning is, By his carriage herein he gained so great an In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terest in the hearts of his People, that they judged most fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vourably of, and put the best construction upon all his words and actions; as, on the contrary, when people have a pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />judice against, or an ill will towards their Prince, they are apt to judge most harshly of all his Counsels and Doings.</ns0:note> pleased all the people.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>f</ns0:hi> Observed what the King said and did.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 For all the people, and all Israel understood that day, that it was not of the King <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not done by his design or good will.</ns0:note> to slay Abner the son of Ner.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 And the king said unto his servants, Know
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:249" />
ye not that there is a prince, and a great man <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Both for his Illustrious Quality, and for his high Cou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rage and wise Conduct; and especially, now for his great usefulness and serviceableness to me in giving me the intire and peaceable Possession of all <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi> But still observe <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi>'s Prudence and Piety, that he doth not commend him for his Vertues and Graces, as men of vendible Consciences and Tongues use to do upon Funeral-occasions; but onely for that kind of worth which was really in him. Compare 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 23.</ns0:note> fallen this day in Israel?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 And I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> this day <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> tender.</ns0:note> weak <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>tender,</ns0:hi> in the Infancy of my Kingdom, not well rooted and settled in it. The Metaphor is taken from a young and tender Child or Plant.</ns0:note>, though anoin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted king; and these men the sons of Zeruiah <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abishai,</ns0:hi> the Sons of my Sister <ns0:hi>Zeruiah.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 19. 7.</ns0:note> too hard for me <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Too powerful. They have so great a command over all the Soldiers, and so great fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour with the People, that I cannot Punish them without apparent hazard to my Person, and Kingdom; especially, now when all the Tribes, except <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> are yet in a state of Opposition against me. But this, although it might give some colour to the delay of their Punishment for a season, yet it may seem to have been one of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s infirmities, that he did not do it within some reasonable time, both because this In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dulgence proceeded from a distrust of Gods Power and Faithfulness; as if God could not, or would not make good his Promise of the Kingdom to him, without, and against <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> and all his Confederates; and because it was contrary to Gods Law, which severely requires the Punishment of Wilful Murderers, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 21. 14. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 35. 21. which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had no power to dispence with.
